segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he came back into Capernaum some days later, word got out that he was at home.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even around the door, and he was speaking the word to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some people came, bringing to him a paralyzed man carried by four of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above where he was, and when they had dug through, they lowered the mat on which the paralyzed man was lying.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Child, your sins are forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, reasoning in their hearts,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins except God alone?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately Jesus, aware in his spirit that they were reasoning this way within themselves, said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you reasoning about these things in your hearts?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which is easier: to say to the paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he said to the paralyzed man,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I say to you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He got up, immediately picked up his mat, and went out in front of everyone, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have never seen anything like this!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went out again beside the sea, and the whole crowd kept coming to him, and he taught them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was passing by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he got up and followed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as he was reclining at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many of them, and they were following him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the scribes of the Pharisees saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On hearing this, Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do John’s disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast, on that day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. Otherwise the patch pulls away from it, the new from the old, and the tear becomes worse.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise the wine will burst the skins, and the wine is lost, and the skins too. Rather, new wine into fresh wineskins.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One Sabbath he was passing through the grainfields, and his disciples began to make their way, plucking the heads of grain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, why are they doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: how he entered the house of God in the time of Abiathar the high priest and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not permitted for anyone but the priests to eat, and gave some also to those who were with him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The Sabbath was made for people, and not people for the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath.”

notes.note: The Greek word names a poor person’s pallet or light stretcher, something one person could roll up and carry. “Bed,” the rendering of the older versions, suggests furniture to a modern reader; most recent translations also use “mat.”

Ordinary Galilean houses had flat roofs of wooden beams covered with branches or reeds and packed clay, reached by an outside stairway or ladder. Opening such a roof meant literally digging through it.

The Greek word means “child” without specifying gender and was used as an affectionate address by an elder or teacher. Most English versions render it “Son” here; the word for “son” in the phrase “Son of Man” (verse 10) is a different one.
Literally “except one, God.” The wording may simply mean “God alone,” or it may deliberately echo Israel’s confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4); the Greek allows either.

This is Jesus’s characteristic way of referring to himself in the Gospels. Behind it lies a Semitic idiom meaning “a human being,” and many scholars also hear an allusion to the figure “like a son of man” who is given authority in Daniel 7:13–14. How much of each sense is intended in a given saying is debated.

Capernaum lay near the border of Herod Antipas’s territory, and Levi was probably collecting tolls or customs duties on goods in transit rather than direct taxes. Such collectors were widely regarded as dishonest and as compromised by their work, which is why they are paired with “sinners” in the next verses.

The Greek does not say whose house this is. Most interpreters take it to be Levi’s, as Luke 5:29 states outright, but Mark’s wording could also mean Jesus’s own home in Capernaum. Guests at a formal meal reclined on couches or cushions rather than sitting.

Many later manuscripts read “the scribes and the Pharisees,” a more familiar phrase, and the older English versions follow them. The earlier and harder reading, adopted here, refers to scribes who belonged to the Pharisaic party.

Literally “the sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic idiom for the bridegroom’s friends and attendants or, more broadly, the guests at the wedding. A wedding celebration could last a week, and fasting during it would have been unthinkable.

The Greek phrase normally means “to make a road,” and a few interpreters think the disciples were clearing a path through the grain. Most take it as equivalent to “make their way,” with the plucking as the point at issue; Deuteronomy 23:25 allowed plucking a neighbor’s grain by hand, so the objection concerns doing it on the Sabbath.

notes.phrase: in the time of Abiathar the high priest
notes.note: In the account in 1 Samuel 21:1–6 the priest who gives David the bread is Ahimelech; Abiathar was his son and became the well-known high priest of David’s reign. The Greek phrase may mean loosely “in the days of Abiathar,” or possibly “in the passage about Abiathar,” and the difficulty is long recognized; Matthew and Luke do not include the phrase.

The traditional “The Sabbath was made for man” uses “man” for humanity in general. The Greek word is the same one found in “Son of Man” in the next verse, so the two sayings are linked. Most interpreters take “Son of Man” there as Jesus’s self-designation, though some think the saying originally meant that human beings have authority over the Sabbath.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels and Acts, and “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers where the word means a trained expert in the Law, so translators vary between “scribe,” “teacher of the law” and “legal expert.”
Recurs throughout the Synoptics, and the choice between “tax collector,” “toll collector” and the older “publican” should be made once.

As a social label in the Gospels (“tax collectors and sinners”) it may mean the notoriously non-observant rather than sinners in the general theological sense, and it needs a consistent rendering and note policy.
Recurs across the New Testament, with translators varying between “authority,” “power” and “right,” and readers would be misled by unexplained variation.
Mark’s signature adverb occurs some forty times and is sometimes only a narrative connective (“then,” “just then”), so a single policy is needed on when to render it “immediately.”

warnings: Verse 7: βλασφημέω is not rendered with a register form (slander; blaspheme; insult / hurl insults at / hurl insults) and has no register-exception note.
